An indictment is a formal, official accusation that a specific person has committed a crime. It is a legal document — or the act of issuing that document — that says, in effect: "There is enough evidence against this person to put them on trial."

The single most important thing to understand right away is this: an indictment is not a conviction. It does not mean the person is guilty. It does not mean they are going to prison. It simply means the justice system has decided there is enough evidence to move forward and hold a proper trial. The person is still presumed innocent until proven guilty in that trial.

Think of it like this: an indictment is the starting gun, not the finish line.
What Exactly Happens When Someone Is Indicted?

In the United States (where this word is most commonly used in its strict legal sense), an indictment typically comes from a grand jury. A grand jury is a group of ordinary citizens — not a judge, not a prosecutor alone — who are gathered specifically to review evidence in serious criminal cases.

Here is the sequence:

  1. A crime is alleged to have occurred.
  2. Prosecutors gather evidence and present it to the grand jury.
  3. The grand jury reviews that evidence in secret — the accused person is not present, and neither is their lawyer.
  4. The grand jury then votes on whether the evidence is strong enough to warrant a formal trial.
  5. If they decide yes, they issue an indictment — officially charging the person with the crime.
  6. The accused person is now said to have been indicted, and the case proceeds to trial.

So the grand jury is essentially acting as a filter. Their job is not to decide guilt or innocence. Their job is simply to ask: "Is there enough here to take this to trial?" If the answer is yes, an indictment is the result.

As a physical document, an indictment typically states:

  • The name of the accused person.
  • The specific crime(s) they are being charged with (e.g., fraud, murder, corruption).
  • A summary of the facts that form the basis of the accusation.
  • The relevant laws that are alleged to have been broken.

It is, in short, the official paperwork that launches a criminal prosecution.

Because this word is so often misunderstood, it helps to be crystal clear about what it is not:

  • It is not a verdict. A verdict (guilty or not guilty) comes at the end of a trial. An indictment comes before a trial even begins.
  • It is not proof of guilt. The evidence reviewed by a grand jury is one-sided — only the prosecution's side is presented. The accused hasn't even had a chance to defend themselves yet.
  • It is not a sentence. No punishment is assigned. No jail time is ordered. It is purely an accusation.
  • It is not the same as an arrest. A person can be arrested before being indicted, or they can be indicted and then arrested, but these are two separate events.

Outside of courtrooms, people also use the word indictment in ordinary conversation to mean a strong, serious criticism that reveals something is deeply wrong or flawed. In this sense, it is used figuratively — not about a legal crime, but about a moral or systemic failure.

For example:

  • "The fact that millions of people go hungry in one of the richest countries in the world is an indictment of its political system."
  • "The school's terrible test scores are an indictment of how underfunded education has become."

In these sentences, no grand jury is involved. Instead, the word is being used to say: "This fact alone is damning evidence that something is seriously wrong." It carries a tone of strong, reasoned condemnation — as though the situation itself is putting something on trial and finding it guilty of failure.

This figurative use borrows its power directly from the legal meaning. Just as a legal indictment says "the evidence against this person is too serious to ignore," the figurative indictment says "the evidence against this system, policy, or situation is too damning to ignore."

Legal use:

  • "The grand jury returned an indictment against the senator on charges of bribery."
  • "Her indictment shocked the entire country, though her lawyers insisted she was innocent."
  • "An indictment was handed down, and the trial is expected to begin in the spring."

Figurative use:

  • "His failure to act in a crisis is a damning indictment of his leadership."
  • "The rising cost of healthcare is an indictment of a broken system."

An indictment is either (1) a formal legal accusation — issued by a grand jury — that officially charges someone with a crime and triggers a criminal trial, while saying nothing about their guilt; or (2) in everyday language, a powerful piece of evidence or argument that something is seriously and fundamentally wrong.
